**Defined:** 2026-02-11
**Core Value:** Showcase technical depth through interactive project demonstrations with comprehensive documentation.

## Milestone v1.1 Requirements

Requirements for adding CPU simulator to portfolio. Each maps to roadmap phases.

### Animation Framework & Data Structures

- [ ] **ANIM-01**: Data structures represent CPU state (pipeline stages, registers, memory, PC)
- [ ] **ANIM-02**: Pre-scripted sequences define program execution step-by-step
- [ ] **ANIM-03**: Animation system can step forward/backward through sequences
- [ ] **ANIM-04**: Program sequences include 8-10 core RISC instructions (add, sub, addi, lw, sw, beq, j)
- [ ] **ANIM-05**: Hazard sequences show data dependencies and stalls
- [ ] **ANIM-06**: Timing system controls animation playback speed

### Interactive Demo

- [ ] **DEMO-01**: Demo page provides step-forward control (advance one animation step)
- [ ] **DEMO-02**: Demo page provides step-backward control (rewind one animation step)
- [ ] **DEMO-03**: Demo page provides play/pause controls with adjustable speed
- [ ] **DEMO-04**: Demo page provides reset control (return to animation start)
- [ ] **DEMO-05**: Demo page provides jump-to-step capability (click on instruction to jump)
- [ ] **DEMO-06**: Demo page includes program selector to switch between examples
- [ ] **DEMO-07**: Demo page includes 2+ pre-scripted programs (basic instructions + Fibonacci)

### Visualization

- [ ] **VIZ-01**: Pipeline stage visualization shows all 5 stages with current instruction in each
- [ ] **VIZ-02**: Register visualization displays all 32 registers with values
- [ ] **VIZ-03**: Register visualization highlights registers that changed in current cycle
- [ ] **VIZ-04**: Memory visualization shows data memory addresses with values
- [ ] **VIZ-05**: Instruction display shows current instruction with field breakdown (opcode, rs, rt, rd, immediate)
- [ ] **VIZ-06**: Execution state displays cycle count and instruction count
- [ ] **VIZ-07**: Hazard visualization highlights data hazards with color-coding
- [ ] **VIZ-08**: Hazard visualization shows stall bubbles in pipeline stages

### Documentation

- [ ] **DOC-01**: Landing page explains CPU project and links to demo + docs
- [ ] **DOC-02**: Pipeline Basics doc page explains 5-stage pipeline concept
- [ ] **DOC-03**: ALU Design doc page explains Carry-Lookahead adder
- [ ] **DOC-04**: Instruction Set doc page documents all implemented instructions
- [ ] **DOC-05**: MultDiv doc page explains Booth's multiplication algorithm
- [ ] **DOC-06**: Advanced Features doc page covers hazards and forwarding
- [ ] **DOC-07**: All doc pages include code snippets from actual Verilog implementation
- [ ] **DOC-08**: All doc pages link to GitHub repo for full source code

### Portfolio Integration

- [ ] **INT-01**: CPU project integrated into portfolio homepage (project card)
- [ ] **INT-02**: CPU demo page uses existing design system (forest green palette)
- [ ] **INT-03**: CPU documentation pages include breadcrumb navigation
- [ ] **INT-04**: CPU pages integrated into site-wide navigation
- [ ] **INT-05**: CPU project follows same structure as graphics engine (demo + docs/)

### Performance & Quality

- [ ] **PERF-01**: Step-through interactions respond in < 100ms
- [ ] **PERF-02**: Demo page loads in < 3 seconds
- [ ] **PERF-03**: Animations maintain 30+ FPS
- [ ] **QUAL-01**: All documentation pages pass WCAG 2.1 AA contrast requirements
- [ ] **QUAL-02**: Demo controls are keyboard-accessible

## Future Requirements (v2.0+)

Deferred to future milestones. Tracked but not in current roadmap.

### Advanced Features
- **ADV-01**: Forwarding visualization showing data bypass paths
- **ADV-02**: Branch prediction visualization
- **ADV-03**: CPI (cycles per instruction) calculation and display
- **ADV-04**: Performance comparison across programs
- **ADV-05**: Export execution trace to JSON/CSV

### Enhanced Interactivity
- **ENH-01**: Breakpoint support (pause at specific instruction)
- **ENH-02**: Watch expressions for register/memory values
- **ENH-03**: Step-over (skip to next instruction in same function)
- **ENH-04**: Custom instruction set editor

## Out of Scope

Explicitly excluded. Documented to prevent scope creep.

| Feature | Reason |
|---------|--------|
| Multi-core simulation | Adds overwhelming complexity, not core to pipeline education |
| Cache hierarchy visualization | Scope creep - v1.1 focuses on pipeline, not memory hierarchy |
| Comprehensive ISA (full MIPS/RISC-V) | 8-10 instructions demonstrate competence without overwhelming |
| Cycle-accurate timing | Not needed for educational visualization |
| Real Verilog execution | Simulating conceptually, not running actual hardware |
| Assembly compiler | Use pre-assembled examples, not building a toolchain |
| Mobile-first responsive | Portfolio is desktop-first, mobile enhancement is v2.0+ |

**Core Value:** Showcase technical depth through interactive project demonstrations with comprehensive documentation.

## Milestone v1.1 Requirements

Requirements for adding CPU simulator to portfolio. Each maps to roadmap phases.

### Animation Framework & Data Structures

- [ ] **ANIM-01**: Data structures represent CPU state (pipeline stages, registers, memory, PC)
- [ ] **ANIM-02**: Pre-scripted sequences define program execution step-by-step
- [ ] **ANIM-03**: Animation system can step forward/backward through sequences
- [ ] **ANIM-04**: Program sequences include 8-10 core RISC instructions (add, sub, addi, lw, sw, beq, j)
- [ ] **ANIM-05**: Hazard sequences show data dependencies and stalls
- [ ] **ANIM-06**: Timing system controls animation playback speed

### Interactive Demo

- [ ] **DEMO-01**: Demo page provides step-forward control (advance one animation step)
- [ ] **DEMO-02**: Demo page provides step-backward control (rewind one animation step)
- [ ] **DEMO-03**: Demo page provides play/pause controls with adjustable speed
- [ ] **DEMO-04**: Demo page provides reset control (return to animation start)

- [ ] **QUAL-01**: All documentation pages pass WCAG 2.1 AA contrast requirements
- [ ] **QUAL-02**: Demo controls are keyboard-accessible

Deferred to future milestones. Tracked but not in current roadmap.

- **ADV-05**: Export execution trace to JSON/CSV

- **ENH-02**: Watch expressions for register/memory values
- **ENH-03**: Step-over (skip to next instruction in same function)
- **ENH-04**: Custom instruction set editor

**Phase description:** 
Phase 11: Interactive Demo Page
**Goal**: Complete demo page with step-through controls for navigating pre-scripted animation sequences
**Depends on**: Phase 10
**Requirements**: DEMO-01, DEMO-02, DEMO-03, DEMO-04, DEMO-05, DEMO-06, DEMO-07, VIZ-04, VIZ-05
**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):
  1. User can step forward and backward through animation frames using step controls
  2. User can play animation with adjustable speed and pause at any frame
  3. User can reset animation to initial state (frame 0)
  4. User can click on any instruction to jump to that point in animation sequence
  5. User can switch between 2+ pre-scripted programs (basic instructions walkthrough + Fibonacci walkthrough)
  6. Memory visualization shows data memory addresses and values as animation progresses
  7. Current instruction displays with field breakdown (opcode, rs, rt, rd, immediate) during walkthrough

**Requirements:** 
DEMO-01: Demo page provides step-forward control (advance one animation step)
DEMO-02: Demo page provides step-backward control (rewind one animation step)
DEMO-03: Demo page provides play/pause controls with adjustable speed
DEMO-04: Demo page provides reset control (return to animation start)
DEMO-05: Demo page provides jump-to-step capability (click on instruction to jump)
DEMO-06: Demo page includes program selector to switch between examples
DEMO-07: Demo page includes 2+ pre-scripted programs (basic instructions + Fibonacci)
VIZ-04: Memory visualization shows data memory addresses with values
VIZ-05: Instruction display shows current instruction with field breakdown (opcode, rs, rt, rd, immediate)

**Prior decisions:** 
- v1.0: Unified forest green design system (#2E7D32 primary)
- v1.0: Vanilla JS + WASM for graphics engine demos
- v1.0: Portfolio-centric navigation with breadcrumbs
- v1.1: CPU simulator will use vanilla JavaScript (no framework)
- v1.1: 5-stage pipeline with hazard detection (8-10 instruction subset)
- v1.1: Follows same structure as graphics engine (demo + docs/)
- 09-01: structuredClone() for state deep copying instead of Object.freeze()
- 09-01: Uint32Array for registers/memory to match 32-bit RISC architecture
- 09-01: Register $0 hardwired to zero via getRegister/setRegister protection
- 09-01: Execute functions compute results without mutating state (pure functions)
- 09-01: Visualization metadata tracked in CPUState for Phase 10+ animation
- 09-02: Base FPS of 2 (500ms per frame at 1x) for educational CPU simulation pacing
- 09-02: Speed range 0.25x-4x with named presets for UI convenience
- 09-02: Generic AnimationEngine design decoupled from CPU state for testability
- 09-02: CustomEvent 'cpu:framechange' on window for loose coupling with UI
- 09-03: Non-pipelined simulation for Phase 9 (each instruction completes all 5 stages before next)
- 09-03: SequenceGenerator clones state per stage, clearing change tracking between stages
- 09-03: Async generateSequenceAsync with 10-instruction chunking for Phase 11+ longer programs
- [Phase 10-01]: Use state.pipeline.IF.instruction for all active stages in non-pipelined mode (avoids duplication)
- [Phase 10-01]: Selective register updates via changedRegisters Set (10x+ performance improvement)
- [Phase 10-01]: CSS transition for register highlight removal (300ms ease-out, respects prefers-reduced-motion)
- [Phase 10-02]: CPUVisualizer coordinator pattern - single entry point manages 3 child views and event wiring
- [Phase 10-02]: aria-live="polite" for execution state accessibility (screen reader announcements)
- [Phase 10-02]: Dual-purpose test page pattern - automated tests + interactive live demo for visual inspection
- [Phase 10-03]: No wire value labels on data paths - keeps diagram clean and educational
- [Phase 10-03]: Native SVG tooltips via <title> elements instead of custom JS library
- [Phase 10-03]: Vertical stacked layout (block diagram full-width, registers below) replaces 2-column grid
</additional_context>

</output>

content.content:
1→---
     2→name: gsd-phase-researcher
     3→description: Researches how to implement a phase before planning. Produces RESEARCH.md consumed by gsd-planner. Spawned by /gsd:plan-phase orchestrator.
     4→tools: Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob, WebSearch, WebFetch, mcp__context7__*
     5→color: cyan
     6→---
     7→
     8→<role>
     9→You are a GSD phase researcher. You answer "What do I need to know to PLAN this phase well?" and produce a single RESEARCH.md that the planner consumes.
    10→
    11→Spawned by `/gsd:plan-phase` (integrated) or `/gsd:research-phase` (standalone).
    12→
    13→**Core responsibilities:**
    14→- Investigate the phase's technical domain
    15→- Identify standard stack, patterns, and pitfalls
    16→- Document findings with confidence levels (HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW)
    17→- Write RESEARCH.md with sections the planner expects
    18→- Return structured result to orchestrator
    19→</role>
    20→
    21→<upstream_input>
    22→**CONTEXT.md** (if exists) — User decisions from `/gsd:discuss-phase`
    23→
    24→| Section | How You Use It |
    25→|---------|----------------|
    26→| `## Decisions` | Locked choices — research THESE, not alternatives |
    27→| `## Claude's Discretion` | Your freedom areas — research options, recommend |
    28→| `## Deferred Ideas` | Out of scope — ignore completely |
    29→
    30→If CONTEXT.md exists, it constrains your research scope. Don't explore alternatives to locked decisions.
    31→</upstream_input>
    32→
    33→<downstream_consumer>
    34→Your RESEARCH.md is consumed by `gsd-planner`:
    35→
    36→| Section | How Planner Uses It |
    37→|---------|---------------------|
    38→| **`## User Constraints`** | **CRITICAL: Planner MUST honor these - copy from CONTEXT.md verbatim** |
    39→| `## Standard Stack` | Plans use these libraries, not alternatives |
    40→| `## Architecture Patterns` | Task structure follows these patterns |
    41→| `## Don't Hand-Roll` | Tasks NEVER build custom solutions for listed problems |
    42→| `## Common Pitfalls` | Verification steps check for these |
    43→| `## Code Examples` | Task actions reference these patterns |
    44→
    45→**Be prescriptive, not exploratory.** "Use X" not "Consider X or Y."
    46→
    47→**CRITICAL:** `## User Constraints` MUST be the FIRST content section in RESEARCH.md. Copy locked decisions, discretion areas, and deferred ideas verbatim from CONTEXT.md.
    48→</downstream_consumer>
    49→
    50→<philosophy>
    51→
    52→## Claude's Training as Hypothesis
    53→
    54→Training data is 6-18 months stale. Treat pre-existing knowledge as hypothesis, not fact.
    55→
    56→**The trap:** Claude "knows" things confidently, but knowledge may be outdated, incomplete, or wrong.
    57→
    58→**The discipline:**
    59→1. **Verify before asserting** — don't state library capabilities without checking Context7 or official docs
    60→2. **Date your knowledge** — "As of my training" is a warning flag
    61→3. **Prefer current sources** — Context7 and official docs trump training data
    62→4. **Flag uncertainty** — LOW confidence when only training data supports a claim
    63→
    64→## Honest Reporting
    65→
    66→Research value comes from accuracy, not completeness theater.
    67→
    68→**Report honestly:**
    69→- "I couldn't find X" is valuable (now we know to investigate differently)
    70→- "This is LOW confidence" is valuable (flags for validation)
    71→- "Sources contradict" is valuable (surfaces real ambiguity)
    72→
    73→**Avoid:** Padding findings, stating unverified claims as facts, hiding uncertainty behind confident language.
    74→
    75→## Research is Investigation, Not Confirmation
    76→
    77→**Bad research:** Start with hypothesis, find evidence to support it
    78→**Good research:** Gather evidence, form conclusions from evidence
    79→
    80→When researching "best library for X": find what the ecosystem actually uses, document tradeoffs honestly, let evidence drive recommendation.
    81→
    82→</philosophy>
    83→
    84→<tool_strategy>
    85→
    86→## Tool Priority
    87→
    88→| Priority | Tool | Use For | Trust Level |
    89→|----------|------|---------|-------------|
    90→| 1st | Context7 | Library APIs, features, configuration, versions | HIGH |
    91→| 2nd | WebFetch | Official docs/READMEs not in Context7, changelogs | HIGH-MEDIUM |
    92→| 3rd | WebSearch | Ecosystem discovery, community patterns, pitfalls | Needs verification |
    93→
    94→**Context7 flow:**
    95→1. `mcp__context7__resolve-library-id` with libraryName
    96→2. `mcp__context7__query-docs` with resolved ID + specific query
    97→
    98→**WebSearch tips:** Always include current year. Use multiple query variations. Cross-verify with authoritative sources.
    99→
   100→## Verification Protocol
   101→
   102→**WebSearch findings MUST be verified:**
   103→
   104→```
   105→For each WebSearch finding:
   106→1. Can I verify with Context7? → YES: HIGH confidence
   107→2. Can I verify with official docs? → YES: MEDIUM confidence
   108→3. Do multiple sources agree? → YES: Increase one level
   109→4. None of the above → Remains LOW, flag for validation
   110→```
   111→
   112→**Never present LOW confidence findings as authoritative.**
   113→
   114→</tool_strategy>
   115→
   116→<source_hierarchy>
   117→
   118→| Level | Sources | Use |
   119→|-------|---------|-----|
   120→| HIGH | Context7, official docs, official releases | State as fact |
   121→| MEDIUM | WebSearch verified with official source, multiple credible sources | State with attribution |
   122→| LOW | WebSearch only, single source, unverified | Flag as needing validation |
   123→
   124→Priority: Context7 > Official Docs > Official GitHub > Verified WebSearch > Unverified WebSearch
   125→
   126→</source_hierarchy>
   127→
   128→<verification_protocol>
   129→
   130→## Known Pitfalls
   131→
   132→### Configuration Scope Blindness
   133→**Trap:** Assuming global configuration means no project-scoping exists
   134→**Prevention:** Verify ALL configuration scopes (global, project, local, workspace)
   135→
   136→### Deprecated Features
   137→**Trap:** Finding old documentation and concluding feature doesn't exist
   138→**Prevention:** Check current official docs, review changelog, verify version numbers and dates
   139→
   140→### Negative Claims Without Evidence
   141→**Trap:** Making definitive "X is not possible" statements without official verification
   142→**Prevention:** For any negative claim — is it verified by official docs? Have you checked recent updates? Are you confusing "didn't find it" with "doesn't exist"?
   143→
   144→### Single Source Reliance
   145→**Trap:** Relying on a single source for critical claims
   146→**Prevention:** Require multiple sources: official docs (primary), release notes (currency), additional source (verification)
   147→
   148→## Pre-Submission Checklist
   149→
   150→- [ ] All domains investigated (stack, patterns, pitfalls)
   151→- [ ] Negative claims verified with official docs
   152→- [ ] Multiple sources cross-referenced for critical claims
   153→- [ ] URLs provided for authoritative sources
   154→- [ ] Publication dates checked (prefer recent/current)
   155→- [ ] Confidence levels assigned honestly
   156→- [ ] "What might I have missed?" review completed
   157→
   158→</verification_protocol>
   159→
   160→<output_format>
   161→
   162→## RESEARCH.md Structure
   163→
   164→**Location:** `.planning/phases/XX-name/{phase}-RESEARCH.md`
   165→
   166→```markdown
   167→# Phase [X]: [Name] - Research
   168→
   169→**Researched:** [date]
   170→**Domain:** [primary technology/problem domain]
   171→**Confidence:** [HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW]
   172→
   173→## Summary
   174→
   175→[2-3 paragraph executive summary]
   176→
   177→**Primary recommendation:** [one-liner actionable guidance]
   178→
   179→## Standard Stack
   180→
   181→### Core
   182→| Library | Version | Purpose | Why Standard |
   183→|---------|---------|---------|--------------|
   184→| [name] | [ver] | [what it does] | [why experts use it] |
   185→
   186→### Supporting
   187→| Library | Version | Purpose | When to Use |
   188→|---------|---------|---------|-------------|
   189→| [name] | [ver] | [what it does] | [use case] |

1→/**
     2→ * Basic Instructions Walkthrough Program
     3→ *
     4→ * Demonstrates all 8 core RISC instruction types through a simple program that:
     5→ * - Loads immediate values into registers
     6→ * - Performs register arithmetic
     7→ * - Executes memory load/store operations
     8→ * - Takes a branch
     9→ * - Performs a jump
    10→ *
    11→ * This program is designed for educational purposes to show how each instruction
    12→ * type behaves in the 5-stage pipeline.
    13→ *
    14→ * Requires: InstructionSet
    15→ */
    16→(function() {
    17→  'use strict';
    18→
    19→  /**
    20→   * Basic Instructions Program
    21→   *
    22→   * Expected final state:
    23→   * - $8 = 10
    24→   * - $9 = 20
    25→   * - $10 = 30 (ADD result)
    26→   * - $11 = 10 (SUB result)
    27→   * - $12 = 30 (LW result)
    28→   * - mem[10] = 30 (SW result)
    29→   */
    30→  const BASIC_PROGRAM = {
    31→    name: "Basic Instructions Walkthrough",
    32→    description: "Demonstrates all 8 core RISC instruction types: register arithmetic, immediates, memory load/store, branch, and jump.",
    33→    instructions: [
    34→      // Step 1: Load immediate values into registers
    35→      Object.assign(
    36→        InstructionSet.createInstruction('ADDI', { rs: 0, rt: 8, immediate: 10 }),
    37→        { comment: 'Load 10 into $8: $8 = $0 + 10' }
    38→      ),
    39→      Object.assign(
    40→        InstructionSet.createInstruction('ADDI', { rs: 0, rt: 9, immediate: 20 }),
    41→        { comment: 'Load 20 into $9: $9 = $0 + 20' }
    42→      ),
    43→
    44→      // Step 2: Register arithmetic
    45→      Object.assign(
    46→        InstructionSet.createInstruction('ADD', { rs: 8, rt: 9, rd: 10 }),
    47→        { comment: 'Add registers: $10 = $8 + $9 = 30' }
    48→      ),
    49→      Object.assign(
    50→        InstructionSet.createInstruction('SUB', { rs: 9, rt: 8, rd: 11 }),
    51→        { comment: 'Subtract registers: $11 = $9 - $8 = 10' }
    52→      ),
    53→
    54→      // Step 3: Memory operations
    55→      Object.assign(
    56→        InstructionSet.createInstruction('SW', { rs: 8, rt: 10, immediate: 0 }),
    57→        { comment: 'Store $10 to memory: mem[$8 + 0] = mem[10] = 30' }
    58→      ),
    59→      Object.assign(
    60→        InstructionSet.createInstruction('LW', { rs: 8, rt: 12, immediate: 0 }),
    61→        { comment: 'Load from memory: $12 = mem[$8 + 0] = mem[10] = 30' }
    62→      ),
    63→
    64→      // Step 4: Branch (taken - skips NOP)
    65→      Object.assign(
    66→        InstructionSet.createInstruction('BEQ', { rs: 8, rt: 8, immediate: 2 }),
    67→        { comment: 'Branch if $8 == $8 (always true): skip 2 instructions ahead' }
    68→      ),
    69→
    70→      // Step 5: NOP (skipped by branch)
    71→      Object.assign(
    72→        InstructionSet.createInstruction('NOP', {}),
    73→        { comment: 'No operation (this instruction is skipped by the branch)' }
    74→      ),
    75→
    76→      // Step 6: Jump (demonstrates J instruction)
    77→      Object.assign(
    78→        InstructionSet.createInstruction('J', { immediate: 0 }),
    79→        { comment: 'Jump to address 0 (demonstrates jump instruction - would loop back)' }
    80→      )
    81→    ]
    82→  };
    83→
    84→  // Export to global scope
    85→  if (typeof window !== 'undefined') {
    86→    window.BASIC_PROGRAM = BASIC_PROGRAM;
    87→  } else if (typeof global !== 'undefined') {
    88→    global.BASIC_PROGRAM = BASIC_PROGRAM;
    89→  }
    90→})();
    91→

1→/**
     2→ * Fibonacci Sequence Program
     3→ *
     4→ * Computes the first 8 Fibonacci numbers (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21) using:
     5→ * - A loop with registers for computation
     6→ * - Memory stores for results
     7→ * - Branch for loop control
     8→ * - Jump for loop iteration
     9→ *
    10→ * This program demonstrates:
    11→ * - Loop structures with branch and jump
    12→ * - Register-based computation
    13→ * - Memory array building
    14→ * - Counter-based loop termination
    15→ *
    16→ * Requires: InstructionSet
    17→ */
    18→(function() {
    19→  'use strict';
    20→
    21→  /**
    22→   * Fibonacci Program
    23→   *
    24→   * Expected final state:
    25→   * - mem[0] = 1 (fib 0)
    26→   * - mem[4] = 1 (fib 1)
    27→   * - mem[8] = 2 (fib 2)
    28→   * - mem[12] = 3 (fib 3)
    29→   * - mem[16] = 5 (fib 4)
    30→   * - mem[20] = 8 (fib 5)
    31→   * - mem[24] = 13 (fib 6)
    32→   * - mem[28] = 21 (fib 7)
    33→   */
    34→  const FIBONACCI_PROGRAM = {
    35→    name: "Fibonacci Sequence",
    36→    description: "Computes the first 8 Fibonacci numbers (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21) using a loop with registers and stores results in memory.",
    37→    instructions: [
    38→      // Initialization: fib(0)=1, fib(1)=1, counter=8, address=0
    39→      Object.assign(
    40→        InstructionSet.createInstruction('ADDI', { rs: 0, rt: 8, immediate: 1 }),
    41→        { comment: 'Initialize $8 = 1 (current Fibonacci number)' }
    42→      ),
    43→      Object.assign(
    44→        InstructionSet.createInstruction('ADDI', { rs: 0, rt: 9, immediate: 1 }),
    45→        { comment: 'Initialize $9 = 1 (next Fibonacci number)' }
    46→      ),
    47→      Object.assign(
    48→        InstructionSet.createInstruction('ADDI', { rs: 0, rt: 10, immediate: 8 }),
    49→        { comment: 'Initialize $10 = 8 (loop counter - compute 8 numbers)' }
    50→      ),
    51→      Object.assign(
    52→        InstructionSet.createInstruction('ADDI', { rs: 0, rt: 11, immediate: 0 }),
    53→        { comment: 'Initialize $11 = 0 (memory address pointer)' }
    54→      ),
    55→
    56→      // Loop body (starts at instruction 4, word address 16)
    57→      Object.assign(
    58→        InstructionSet.createInstruction('SW', { rs: 11, rt: 8, immediate: 0 }),
    59→        { comment: 'Store current Fibonacci: mem[$11] = $8' }
    60→      ),
    61→      Object.assign(
    62→        InstructionSet.createInstruction('ADD', { rs: 8, rt: 9, rd: 12 }),
    63→        { comment: 'Compute next Fibonacci: $12 = $8 + $9' }
    64→      ),
    65→      Object.assign(
    66→        InstructionSet.createInstruction('ADD', { rs: 9, rt: 0, rd: 8 }),
    67→        { comment: 'Shift values: $8 = $9 (current = next)' }
    68→      ),
    69→      Object.assign(
    70→        InstructionSet.createInstruction('ADD', { rs: 12, rt: 0, rd: 9 }),
    71→        { comment: 'Shift values: $9 = $12 (next = computed)' }
    72→      ),
    73→      Object.assign(
    74→        InstructionSet.createInstruction('ADDI', { rs: 11, rt: 11, immediate: 4 }),
    75→        { comment: 'Advance memory pointer: $11 = $11 + 4 (one word)' }
    76→      ),
    77→      Object.assign(
    78→        InstructionSet.createInstruction('ADDI', { rs: 10, rt: 10, immediate: -1 }),
    79→        { comment: 'Decrement counter: $10 = $10 - 1' }
    80→      ),
    81→      Object.assign(
    82→        InstructionSet.createInstruction('BEQ', { rs: 10, rt: 0, immediate: 1 }),
    83→        { comment: 'Branch if done: if $10 == 0, skip to end (offset +1)' }
    84→      ),
    85→      Object.assign(
    86→        InstructionSet.createInstruction('J', { immediate: 4 }),
    87→        { comment: 'Jump back to loop body: jump to word address 4 (instruction 4)' }
    88→      ),
    89→
    90→      // End
    91→      Object.assign(
    92→        InstructionSet.createInstruction('NOP', {}),
    93→        { comment: 'End of program' }
    94→      )
    95→    ]
    96→  };
    97→
    98→  // Export to global scope
    99→  if (typeof window !== 'undefined') {
   100→    window.FIBONACCI_PROGRAM = FIBONACCI_PROGRAM;
   101→  } else if (typeof global !== 'undefined') {
   102→    global.FIBONACCI_PROGRAM = FIBONACCI_PROGRAM;
   103→  }
   104→
   105→  // Also export program registry
   106→  if (typeof window !== 'undefined') {
   107→    window.CPU_PROGRAMS = {
   108→      basic: window.BASIC_PROGRAM,
   109→      fibonacci: FIBONACCI_PROGRAM
   110→    };
   111→  } else if (typeof global !== 'undefined') {
   112→    global.CPU_PROGRAMS = {
   113→      basic: global.BASIC_PROGRAM,
   114→      fibonacci: FIBONACCI_PROGRAM
   115→    };
   116→  }
   117→})();

**Phase description:** 
Phase 11: Interactive Demo Page
**Goal**: Complete demo page with step-through controls for navigating pre-scripted animation sequences
**Depends on**: Phase 10
**Requirements**: DEMO-01, DEMO-02, DEMO-03, DEMO-04, DEMO-05, DEMO-06, DEMO-07, VIZ-04, VIZ-05
**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):
  1. User can step forward and backward through animation frames using step controls
  2. User can play animation with adjustable speed and pause at any frame
  3. User can reset animation to initial state (frame 0)
  4. User can click on any instruction to jump to that point in animation sequence
  5. User can switch between 2+ pre-scripted programs (basic instructions walkthrough + Fibonacci walkthrough)
  6. Memory visualization shows data memory addresses and values as animation progresses
  7. Current instruction displays with field breakdown (opcode, rs, rt, rd, immediate) during walkthrough

**Requirements:** 
DEMO-01: Demo page provides step-forward control (advance one animation step)
DEMO-02: Demo page provides step-backward control (rewind one animation step)
DEMO-03: Demo page provides play/pause controls with adjustable speed
DEMO-04: Demo page provides reset control (return to animation start)
DEMO-05: Demo page provides jump-to-step capability (click on instruction to jump)
DEMO-06: Demo page includes program selector to switch between examples
DEMO-07: Demo page includes 2+ pre-scripted programs (basic instructions + Fibonacci)
VIZ-04: Memory visualization shows data memory addresses with values
VIZ-05: Instruction display shows current instruction with field breakdown (opcode, rs, rt, rd, immediate)

**Prior decisions:** 
- v1.0: Unified forest green design system (#2E7D32 primary)
- v1.0: Vanilla JS + WASM for graphics engine demos
- v1.0: Portfolio-centric navigation with breadcrumbs
- v1.1: CPU simulator will use vanilla JavaScript (no framework)
- v1.1: 5-stage pipeline with hazard detection (8-10 instruction subset)
- v1.1: Follows same structure as graphics engine (demo + docs/)
- 09-01: structuredClone() for state deep copying instead of Object.freeze()
- 09-01: Uint32Array for registers/memory to match 32-bit RISC architecture
- 09-01: Register $0 hardwired to zero via getRegister/setRegister protection
- 09-01: Execute functions compute results without mutating state (pure functions)
- 09-01: Visualization metadata tracked in CPUState for Phase 10+ animation
- 09-02: Base FPS of 2 (500ms per frame at 1x) for educational CPU simulation pacing
- 09-02: Speed range 0.25x-4x with named presets for UI convenience
- 09-02: Generic AnimationEngine design decoupled from CPU state for testability
- 09-02: CustomEvent 'cpu:framechange' on window for loose coupling with UI
- 09-03: Non-pipelined simulation for Phase 9 (each instruction completes all 5 stages before next)
- 09-03: SequenceGenerator clones state per stage, clearing change tracking between stages
- 09-03: Async generateSequenceAsync with 10-instruction chunking for Phase 11+ longer programs
- [Phase 10-01]: Use state.pipeline.IF.instruction for all active stages in non-pipelined mode (avoids duplication)
- [Phase 10-01]: Selective register updates via changedRegisters Set (10x+ performance improvement)
- [Phase 10-01]: CSS transition for register highlight removal (300ms ease-out, respects prefers-reduced-motion)
- [Phase 10-02]: CPUVisualizer coordinator pattern - single entry point manages 3 child views and event wiring
- [Phase 10-02]: aria-live="polite" for execution state accessibility (screen reader announcements)
- [Phase 10-02]: Dual-purpose test page pattern - automated tests + interactive live demo for visual inspection
- [Phase 10-03]: No wire value labels on data paths - keeps diagram clean and educational
- [Phase 10-03]: Native SVG tooltips via <title> elements instead of custom JS library
- [Phase 10-03]: Vertical stacked layout (block diagram full-width, registers below) replaces 2-column grid
</additional_context>

<output>
Write to: .planning/phases/11-interactive-demo-page/11-RESEARCH.md
</output>

1→/*
     2→ * Design System - Single Source of Truth for Visual Tokens
     3→ *
     4→ * This file defines all design tokens (colors, spacing, typography, animation)
     5→ * as CSS custom properties. All pages in the portfolio link to this file.
     6→ *
     7→ * Usage: var(--color-primary), var(--space-md), var(--text-lg), etc.
     8→ */
     9→
    10→:root {
    11→  /* ============================================
    12→   * COLOR PALETTE - Unified Green Theme
    13→   * ============================================ */
    14→
    15→  /* Primary Colors (Forest Green) */
    16→  --color-primary: #2E7D32;           /* Forest green - AA contrast 4.98:1 on white */
    17→  --color-primary-dark: #1B5E20;      /* Dark forest green - AA contrast 8.59:1 on white */
    18→
    19→  /* Accent Colors (Light Green) */
    20→  --color-accent: #4CAF50;            /* Light green - for dark backgrounds only */
    21→  --color-accent-light: #81C784;      /* Pastel green - borders/subtle highlights */
    22→
    23→  /* Surface Colors */
    24→  --color-surface: #ffffff;           /* Primary background */
    25→  --color-surface-alt: #f8f9fa;       /* Secondary background */
    26→  --color-surface-dim: #f5f5f5;       /* Tertiary background */
    27→
    28→  /* Text Colors */
    29→  --color-text: #333333;              /* Body text */
    30→  --color-text-heading: #2c3e50;      /* Headings */
    31→  --color-text-muted: #666666;        /* Secondary text */
    32→  --color-text-light: #555555;        /* Tertiary text */
    33→
    34→  /* Border Colors */
    35→  --color-border: #e0e0e0;            /* Primary borders */
    36→  --color-border-light: #dddddd;      /* Light borders */
    37→
    38→  /* Special Purpose Colors */
    39→  --color-code-bg: #1e1e1e;           /* Code block background */
    40→  --color-footer-bg: #2c3e50;         /* Footer background */

    51→   * ============================================ */
    52→
    53→  --space-xs: 0.5rem;     /* 8px - Minimal spacing */

    57→  --space-xl: 3.25rem;    /* 52px - Extra large spacing */
    58→
    59→  /* ============================================
    60→   * TYPOGRAPHY
    61→   * ============================================ */
    62→
    63→  /* Font Families */
    64→  --font-body: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Oxygen, Ubuntu, Cantarell, sans-serif;
    65→  --font-mono: 'Monaco', 'Menlo', 'Ubuntu Mono', 'Consolas', monospace;
    66→
    67→  /* Font Sizes (Fluid Typography with clamp) */
    68→  --text-xs: clamp(0.75rem, 0.7rem + 0.25vw, 0.875rem);      /* 12px - 14px */
    69→  --text-sm: clamp(0.875rem, 0.8rem + 0.4vw, 1rem);          /* 14px - 16px */
    70→  --text-base: clamp(1rem, 0.95rem + 0.25vw, 1.125rem);      /* 16px - 18px */
    71→  --text-lg: clamp(1.125rem, 1rem + 0.6vw, 1.5rem);          /* 18px - 24px */
    72→  --text-xl: clamp(1.5rem, 1.2rem + 1.5vw, 2.5rem);          /* 24px - 40px */
    73→
    74→  /* Line Heights */
    75→  --leading-body: 1.6;        /* Body text readability */
    76→  --leading-heading: 1.2;     /* Tight heading spacing */
    77→  --leading-code: 1.4;        /* Code block readability */

The user has decided to replace the simple "IF: ADD $t0, $t1, $t2" stage cards with a hardware block diagram showing functional units (Instruction Memory, Register File, ALU, Data Memory), pipeline registers (F/D, D/X, X/M, M/W), multiplexers, and data flow paths. The visualization will show which instruction is in each pipeline stage, highlight active components, and display register values via tooltips.

Standard SVG primitives (`<rect>`, `<polygon>`, `<text>`, `<g>`) combined with proper namespace handling (`createElementNS`) deliver performant interactive diagrams.

   101→
   102→### Recommended Project Structure
   103→```
   104→cpu-simulator/src/visualization/

   111→
   112→### Pattern 1: SVG Component Creation with Namespace
   113→
   114→**What:** Use `createElementNS` with correct SVG namespace for all SVG element creation
   115→
   116→**When to use:** Every time you create SVG elements dynamically (`<svg>`, `<rect>`, `<text>`, `<g>`, `<polygon>`, etc.)
   117→
   118→**Example:**
   119→```javascript
   120→// Source: MDN - Namespaces crash course
   121→// https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/SVG/Namespaces_Crash_Course
   122→
   123→const SVG_NS = 'http://www.w3.org/2000/svg';
   124→
   125→function createSVGElement(tagName, attributes = {}) {
   126→  const element = document.createElementNS(SVG_NS, tagName);
   127→
   128→  // Set attributes (no namespace for most SVG attributes)
   129→  Object.entries(attributes).forEach(([key, value]) => {
   130→    element.setAttribute(key, value);
   131→  });
   132→
   133→  return element;
   134→}
   135→
   136→// Usage
   137→const rect = createSVGElement('rect', {
   138→  x: 10,
   139→  y: 10,
   140→  width: 100,
   141→  height: 50,
   142→  class: 'alu-component'
   143→});
   144→```
   145→
   146→**Critical:** Use `setAttribute()` not `setAttributeNS()` for standard SVG attributes (x, y, width, height, class). Only use `setAttributeNS()` for namespaced attributes like `xlink:href`.

1→# Phase 9: Animation Framework & Data Structures - Research
     2→
     3→**Researched:** 2026-02-11
     4→**Domain:** JavaScript animation systems, CPU pipeline simulation, state management
     5→**Confidence:** HIGH
     6→
     7→## Summary
     8→
     9→Phase 9 establishes the foundational animation framework and data structures for a CPU pipeline simulator that steps through pre-scripted instruction sequences. The phase requires implementing data structures to represent 5-stage pipeline state (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB), 32 RISC registers, memory, and program counter, along with an animation system that can step forward/backward through execution frames and control playback speed.
    10→
    11→Research reveals that modern JavaScript (2026) provides excellent native capabilities for this task. The Web Animations API offers timeline control (play, pause, reverse, currentTime) but is optimized for DOM animations, not state snapshots. For CPU simulation, a custom frame-based approach using `requestAnimationFrame` provides better control over discrete state transitions. Industry patterns favor immutable state snapshots for reliable undo/redo, where each animation frame represents a complete CPU state that can be navigated bidirectionally.
    12→
    13→Existing CPU simulators (Y86, WebRISC-V, Interactive RISC-V Simulator) demonstrate that successful educational simulators use explicit state objects with pipeline registers, instruction queues, and memory arrays. The standard pattern uses arrays of state snapshots with integer frame indices, enabling instant jumps and bidirectional stepping. Performance analysis shows `structuredClone()` (native as of 2021, optimized by 2026) outperforms JSON.parse/stringify for deep cloning state objects, achieving <1ms clones for typical CPU state (~100KB).
    14→
    15→**Primary recommendation:** Build a custom frame-based animation system using an array of immutable state snapshots (created with `structuredClone()`), indexed by frame number, with playback controlled via `requestAnimationFrame` and delta-time calculations. Pre-generate all animation frames during program load to enable instant bidirectional navigation and frame jumps.
    16→
    17→## Standard Stack
    18→
    19→### Core
    20→
    21→| Library/Technology | Version | Purpose | Why Standard |
    22→|-------------------|---------|---------|--------------|

    52→### Recommended Project Structure
    53→
    54→```
    55→cpu-simulator/

    57→├── src/

    64→│   │   ├── sequence-loader.js   # Pre-scripted program sequences

    80→```javascript

    82→// Influenced by: https://github.com/kevinnayar/temporis
    83→// https://macwright.com/2015/05/18/practical-undo
    84→
    85→class CPUState {
    86→  constructor() {
    87→    // Pipeline stage registers (IF/ID, ID/EX, EX/MEM, MEM/WB)
    88→    this.pipeline = {
    89→      IF: { instruction: 0, pc: 0 },
    90→      ID: { instruction: 0, opcode: 0, rs: 0, rt: 0, rd: 0, imm: 0 },
    91→      EX: { aluResult: 0, writeData: 0, writeReg: 0 },
    92→      MEM: { memData: 0, writeData: 0, writeReg: 0 },
    93→      WB: { writeData: 0, writeReg: 0 }
    94→    };
    95→
    96→    // Register file (32 registers, 32-bit each)
    97→    this.registers = new Uint32Array(32);
    98→
    99→    // Data memory (256 words = 1KB for demo)
   100→    this.memory = new Uint32Array(256);
   101→
   102→    // Control state
   103→    this.pc = 0;              // Program counter
   104→    this.cycleCount = 0;      // Total cycles executed
   105→    this.instructionCount = 0; // Instructions completed
   106→
   107→    // Metadata for visualization
   108→    this.changedRegisters = new Set(); // Track which regs changed this cycle
   109→    this.hazards = [];        // Active hazards this cycle
   110→  }

   113→  clone() {

   116→    Object.freeze(cloned.pipeline);
   117→    Object.freeze(cloned.pipeline.IF);
   118→    Object.freeze(cloned.pipeline.ID);
   119→    Object.freeze(cloned.pipeline.EX);
   120→    Object.freeze(cloned.pipeline.MEM);
   121→    Object.freeze(cloned.pipeline.WB);
   122→    return cloned;
   123→  }
   124→}

   128→- Immutability prevents accidental state corruption during animation
   129→- Enables instant jump to any frame (no need to replay from start)
   130→- Supports bidirectional stepping without complex undo logic
   131→- Object.freeze() adds zero runtime cost in production, catches bugs in dev
   132→
   133→### Pattern 2: Frame-Based Animation Controller

   135→**What:** Pre-generate all animation frames, store in array, navigate by index
   136→**When to use:** For all pre-scripted animation sequences

   142→// javascript.info: https://javascript.info/js-animation

   144→class AnimationEngine {
   145→  constructor() {
   146→    this.frames = [];           // Array of CPUState snapshots
   147→    this.currentFrame = 0;      // Current frame index
   148→    this.isPlaying = false;     // Playback state

I've completed the web search for educational animation controls step through frames UI UX patterns 2026. Here are the key findings:

## Key UI/UX Trends for Educational Animation Controls in 2026

**Motion-Driven Interaction Patterns:**
Motion design isn't just about smooth transitions anymore, with tools like LottieFiles introducing state machines that allow animations to change based on logic. Designers can define interactions without relying on developers.

**Micro-Interactions for Step-Through Controls:**
Micro-interactions are meant to be light and fast, with the ideal duration between 200 and 500 milliseconds—long enough to be noticed, yet short enough to maintain flow. Motion helps users follow transitions between states, understand the outcome of an action, or feel reassured when a task completes.

**Educational Content & Animation:**
Spatial storytelling involves interfaces that guide users through a "space" rather than a flat scroll, which museum exhibits, educational content, and product launches use effectively. Animated, scroll-based storytelling helps users understand complex information at a glance, with some financial and analytics platforms using animated story flows that guide users through insights step by step.

**Tool Developments:**
Rive and tools like Framer now support 3D interactions without code, allowing designers to add hover states, pressed animations, and spatial responses.

**Accessibility Considerations:**
Motion must be inclusive, with not every user experiencing animation comfortably; users should have the option to reduce or disable motion.

## Modern HTML5 Media Controls Patterns for 2026

**Core Control Architecture:**
Custom media players involve a media element (the engine), a UI layer (the cockpit), and a thin controller in JavaScript (the wiring).

**Essential Controls:**
Modern video players should include play/pause, skip, seek/scrub, current time + duration, mute/volume, keyboard controls, and a control bar that shows on interaction and hides when watching.

**Step Forward/Backward Implementation:**
Custom actions like skip intro and replay 15s are recommended features for contemporary video players.

**UI/Accessibility Best Practices:**
Developers become responsible for basic usability: keyboard access, focus order, readable contrast, and touch targets.

**Control Visibility Patterns:**
A well-implemented control bar appears only when the user needs it, which improves the viewing experience.

**Additional Modern Features:**
Captions should be included - they help in loud offices, quiet trains, and accessibility contexts. Playback speed control (1.25×–2×) is considered a daily driver for tutorials and meetings.

**JavaScript API Approach:**
Custom players replace the browser's default controls with custom UI while connecting that UI to the HTMLMediaElement API, allowing consistency across all modern browsers.

Based on the search results, here's information about memory viewer hex address value display patterns and UI designs:

## Memory Viewer UI Components

A hex dump is a textual hexadecimal view of computer data from memory, where each byte is represented as a two-digit hexadecimal number and are commonly organized into rows of 8 or 16 bytes, sometimes separated by whitespaces.

## Standard Display Pattern

Memory viewers typically employ a table/grid layout with the following elements:

- **Address Column**: Some hex dumps have the hexadecimal memory address at the beginning. The address is displayed in hex format, and the memory is also shown in hex format, each byte separated by a space.

- **Value Columns**: An ASCII representation of the memory is shown on the right side.

## Interactive Features

Modern memory viewers include several UI patterns for interaction:

- **Navigation**: The address input shows the current byte address in hex format, and you can input a new value to jump to a new location in the memory buffer.

- **Value Formatting**: You can switch between dec, hex, oct for integer and sci, dec for floats.

- **Data Type Previews**: Modern hex viewers offer viewing and editing capabilities with real-time change highlighting, data type previews, and comprehensive navigation features for detailed memory analysis.

These patterns represent established standards in memory visualization tools used across debugging platforms, hex editors, and development environments.

Based on the web search results, here's a comprehensive overview of RISC instruction field breakdown for educational visualization:

## RISC Instruction Format Overview

RISC-V instruction formats have a fixed length of 32 bits, and they contain several key fields that are essential to understand:

### Core Instruction Fields

**Opcode Field**
The 7 bits from 0 to 6 are opcode (operation code), used to identify the type of instruction. The opcode field is the primary indicator of an instruction's general category or type, in particular, it distinguishes between the R, I, S, B, U, and J type instruction families.

**Register Fields**
Bits 7 to 11 are the index of the rd register. The rd register is also called the destination register, and the destination register is the register used to store the result. The index of rs1 is in bits 15-19, and the index of rs2 is in bits 20-24.

**Function Fields**
The 3-bit funct3 field distinguishes operations with a given opcode category. The 7-bit funct7 field distinguishes operations that share an opcode category and funct3 value; for example, the add and sub instructions.

### Instruction Format Types

Different instruction formats organize these fields differently:

- **R-type**: R-type instructions specify two source registers (rs1 and rs2) and a destination register (rd)
- **I-type**: I-type instructions have a result register (rd), a source register for one of its operands (rs1), and 12-bit immediate value for the other operand
- **S-type**: The S-type format is used for control and memory instructions (in particular, store instructions). An S-type instruction has no rd register
- **U-type**: The U format has the smallest number of fields out of all core instruction formats, only supporting opcode, rd, and a 20 bit immediate

For detailed visual diagrams and hex encoding examples, the RISC-V specification and educational resources like the GitHub RISC-V opcodes repository contain comprehensive breakdowns of how these fields are positioned within the 32-bit instruction word.
